rows.visible_answer: The PostgreSQL 17.11 “app-initdb” documentation's “Options” section covers less commonly used options, including: forcibly setting a server parameter name to a value during initdb and installing that setting in the generated postgresql.conf so it applies during future server runs (can be given more than once, primarily useful when the server will not start at all with default parameters); printing debugging output from the bootstrap backend and other minor messages; running the bootstrap backend with debug_discard_caches=1 (very slow, only for deep debugging); specifying where initdb should find its input files; inhibiting cleanup of files created when initdb fails (useful for debugging); and returning without waiting for files to be written safely to disk (faster but risks corruption after an OS crash, so not for production). The synopsis shows the basic form: initdb [option...] [ --pgdata | -D ] directory.

The supplied evidence does not include the “Environment” section of the app-initdb documentation, so I cannot state what it says. The evidence covers the Environment sections of other utilities (pgreceivewal, pgcombinebackup, pgbasebackup, pgrestore, pgdump, pg_dumpall), which note libpq environment variables and PG_COLOR, but none of these is app-initdb.

The supplied evidence does not contain an "Environment" section for pg_ctl, so I cannot describe what PG-CTL is used for in that section. The evidence does describe pg_ctl generally: it is a utility for initializing a PostgreSQL database cluster, starting, stopping, or restarting the server, or displaying server status (E04, E05). The "Environment" sections present in the evidence belong to other utilities (pgreceivewal, pgcombinebackup, pgbasebackup) and state that those utilities use libpq environment variables and that PG_COLOR controls color in diagnostic messages (E01, E02, E03); this is not stated for pg_ctl in the provided evidence.

In the “Files” section of the pg_ctl documentation, the file described is the postmaster.pid file in the data directory. pg_ctl examines this file to determine whether the server is currently running. If the file exists, pg_ctl in restart mode passes its contents as options to postgres, unless overridden by the -o option, and the file's contents are also displayed in status mode.

The evidence does not contain enough information to summarize both a “Notes” section and a “Description” section for PostgreSQL 17.11. The only “Notes” section supplied is from the SQL PREPARE documentation, which states that you can see all prepared statements available in the session by querying the pg_prepared_statements system view (E08). No “Description” section is included in the provided evidence, so it cannot be summarized.

pg_combinebackup (PostgreSQL 17.11) reconstructs a full backup from an incremental backup and the earlier backups it depends on. You specify all required backups on the command line from oldest to newest — the first directory being the full backup and the last the final incremental backup — and the reconstructed backup is written to the output directory given by -o. It attempts to verify that the specified backups form a legal backup chain, but it does not track backup dependencies for you, and it only checks the relationship between backups, not whether each individual backup is intact (use pg_verifybackup for that). Because its output is a synthetic full backup, it can itself be used as input to a future pg_combinebackup invocation in place of the original chain.

Regarding options: the documented options include disabling generation of a backup manifest (otherwise a manifest for the reconstructed backup is written to the output directory); a sync option whose default is fsync, which recursively opens and synchronizes all files in the backup directory (following symbolic links for the WAL directory and each configured tablespace in plain format), with syncfs available on Linux to synchronize the whole containing file system (and, in plain format, the file systems containing WAL files and each tablespace), noting the caveats described under recovery_init_sync_method; this option has no effect when --no-sync is used. There are also options to print the pg_combinebackup version and exit, and to show help about command-line arguments and exit. Note that the supplied evidence excerpt for the Options section does not include the option names/flags themselves, so those cannot be stated from this evidence.

The supplied evidence does not contain a documentation section specifically titled “Options” for either version, so a direct section-by-section comparison of such a page cannot be made. What the evidence does show for both 17.11 and 18.6 is consistent: (1) In Appendix C (SQL Key Words), OPTION and OPTIONS are listed as non-reserved in PostgreSQL in both versions, with OPTION non-reserved in SQL:2023/SQL:2016 and reserved in SQL-92, and OPTIONS non-reserved in SQL:2023/SQL:2016 (E02, E05). (2) The ALTER FOREIGN TABLE synopsis in both versions includes OPTIONS ( [ ADD | SET | DROP ] option ['value'] [, ... ] ) for both column-level and table-level options (E07, E08). (3) The configure “Anti-Features” section in both versions describes options that disable default features (ICU, Readline/libedit, Zlib), with the 17.11 text additionally mentioning spinlock and atomic-operation options (E01, E06). No differences between the two frozen versions on these points are evidenced.

The supplied evidence does not contain any documentation section titled "Notes" for either PostgreSQL 17.11 or 18.6, so I cannot state what each frozen version says about it. The evidence consists only of excerpts from Appendix C (SQL Key Words) for both versions (e.g., entries for FIRST/FROM, TABLE/TIME, NFKD/NULLS, CONNECTION/COPARTITION, and OVERRIDING/PARTIAL) plus a psql text-search support page for 17.11. None of these excerpts is a "Notes" section, and no comparison of such a section can be made from them.

The supplied evidence does not cover Python virtual environments. It only describes build-time requirements for PL/Python: you need a Python installation with header files and the sysconfig module, and libpython must be a shared library (configure fails if it cannot find one; when building Python from source, use --enable-shared). The minimum Python version differs by PostgreSQL version: 3.2 for PostgreSQL 17 and 3.6.8 for PostgreSQL 18. For virtual-environment setup guidance, consult other documentation.

rows.visible_answer: No evidence supports the premise. PostgreSQL does not store tables in a blockchain; the supplied evidence contains no such claim. The freezing section (19.10.4) describes how VACUUM marks sufficiently old rows as frozen to maintain correctness after transaction ID wraparound, and how aggressive scans are triggered based on pg_class.relfrozenxid age (default 150 million transactions, effectively limited to 95% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age). It says nothing about blockchain storage. The premise appears to be false, and no cited section proves it.

No PostgreSQL section proves that premise, because it is false. VACUUM does not convert SQL into Java bytecode. The freezing documentation describes VACUUM marking sufficiently old rows as frozen so they are visible to everyone without examining the inserting XID, and it describes aggressive scans when pg_class.relfrozenxid reaches the configured age (default 150 million transactions, silently limited to 95% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age). Nothing in the supplied evidence mentions Java or bytecode.

The supplied evidence does not document the behavior of SELECT, and none of it is from PostgreSQL 9.0. The evidence covers type conversion overview (10.1), FETCH and DECLARE cursor notes/parameters, XML predicates such as xml_is_well_formed, and system catalog information functions, for versions 17.11 and 18.6 only. Therefore the exact documented behavior of SELECT in PostgreSQL 9.0 cannot be determined from this evidence.

The evidence covers only PostgreSQL 17.11 and 18.6, and none of it documents the SELECT command itself; the closest related material is about type conversion in expressions (E01, E02), cursors/FETCH (E03, E04, E09, E10), XML predicates (E05, E06), and system catalog information functions (E07, E08). To answer for 9.1, the SELECT reference page for that version would be needed.

The evidence does not contain a single, general statement of PostgreSQL's "default authentication behavior," and no version was specified, so a version-specific answer cannot be selected. What the evidence does show: client authentication is controlled by the pg_hba.conf file (traditionally in the cluster's data directory), and a default pg_hba.conf is installed when initdb initializes the data directory (E04, E05). The file is read at start-up and on SIGHUP; on Windows, changes are applied immediately to subsequent new connections (E04, E05). The pg_hba_file_rules view can be used to pre-test changes or diagnose problems (E04, E05). Related authentication settings in the evidence include a parameter controlling whether a WARNING about MD5 password deprecation is produced (default on), Kerberos key file location, GSSAPI case-insensitivity (default off), and GSSAPI delegation (default off) (E07). The evidence does not specify which authentication method the default pg_hba.conf entries use, so that cannot be stated here.

No version was specified, so here is the option list as documented for PostgreSQL 18 (the same option set appears in the 17 documentation). Per the VACUUM synopsis, the options are: FULL [ boolean ], FREEZE [ boolean ], VERBOSE [ boolean ], ANALYZE [ boolean ], DISABLE_PAGE_SKIPPING [ boolean ], SKIP_LOCKED [ boolean ], INDEX_CLEANUP { AUTO | ON | OFF }, PROCESS_MAIN [ boolean ], PROCESS_TOAST [ boolean ], TRUNCATE [ boolean ], PARALLEL integer, SKIP_DATABASE_STATS [ boolean ], ONLY_DATABASE_STATS [ boolean ], and BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT size. Options are given in parentheses after VACUUM, e.g. VACUUM (option [, ...]) [ table_and_columns [, ...] ]. Boolean options accept TRUE/ON/1 or FALSE/OFF/0, and if the boolean value is omitted, TRUE is assumed. The older pre-9.0 syntax (VACUUM [ FULL ] [ FREEZE ] [ VERBOSE ] [ ANALYZE ] [ table_and_columns]) is still supported but requires options in exactly that order. Note: the evidence covers versions 17 and 18 only; behavior in other versions is not shown here.
